newsitem.title: USA: Nicaraguan immigrants suing United States.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan immigrants suing United States.

text.p: Thousands of Nicaraguans who fled a U.S.-backed war in their homeland have been illegally denied residency in the United States and are now threatened with deportation, a lawsuit alleged on Wednesday.

The lawsuit, to be filed early on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Miami, alleges that U.S. presidents from Jimmy Carter to Bill Clinton failed to grant Nicaraguans refugee status, leaving them in immigration limbo while allowing them to work and pay taxes here.

As a result, at least 50,000 Nicaraguans now living in the United States will be threatened with deportation because of changes in U.S. immigration laws due to take effect on April 1, attorney Alfonso Oviedo-Reyes said.

"The Nicaraguans should have been granted status as refugees at the beginning of the time when they began coming to the United States," he said. "For reasons of political expediency they were not granted that status."

The suit, which names as defendants President Bill Clinton, Attorney General Janet Reno and Immigration Commissioner Doris Meissner, claims class-action status on behalf of about 50,000 Nicaraguans, most of them living in Miami.

The lawsuit asks the court to rule that the U.S. government violated the constitutional rights of the refugees and to grant "orderly determination" of their asylum claims. Oviedo-Reyes also said he would seek an emergency injunction to halt deportations.

Community leaders say thousands of Nicaraguans, some of whom have lived in the United States for more than 10 years, were living in fear of deportation orders and raids by immigration agents because of the April 1 deadline, when a law which tightens the process of appeals against deportation comes into effect.
Some of the refugees are ex-guerrillas who fought for the Contra army in a war against Nicaragua's leftist Sandinista government in the 1980s.

"We gave our blood. They used Nicaraguans to protect America, and now they want us to leave," said Nora Britton, director of Fraternidad Nicaraguense, a coalition of exile groups and a plaintiff in the lawsuit. "This is discrimination. Maybe it is because of the way we look."
The lawsuit alleged that U.S. immigration reforms will deny due process to Nicaraguans who have been legally living and working in the United States for years.

"The underlying political situations that gave rise to the Contra War and the exodus of the plaintiffs from their homeland were so intimately connected to U.S. foreign policy that the plaintiffs should have been (granted) the status of of refugees in the United States," it said.
